subtype: Approach: rushing to finish before the deadline [Pitfall]
passage: Darshan carried his science model into class in a carton this morning, and before he reached his desk the roof slid off and the walls folded like a wet paper bag. Yesterday he had told me he would start after dinner, and he only found the glue at ten at night. He glued the walls wet and went to bed. The glue had not set. He looked at the heap on his desk and said nothing. I don't know if he was angrier with himself or with the glue. I helped pick up the pieces. - Suraj

qa.q: When did Darshan start building the model?
qa.a: He started after dinner the night before, and found the glue at ten at night.

qa.q: What might Darshan have been feeling as he looked at the heap on his desk?
qa.a: Upset and embarrassed, possibly angry with himself, though Suraj cannot tell which.

qa.q: What could Darshan do next time with a deadline, and why?
qa.a: He could start earlier and leave time for the glue to dry, so the model has set before it has to be carried.

qa.q: How does Suraj see the collapse?
qa.a: Suraj is sympathetic and helps pick up the pieces, without knowing exactly what Darshan felt.

grounding: A boy leaves his science model until the night before and glues it wet, and it falls apart in the morning.

subtype: Approach: rushing to finish before the deadline [Pitfall]
passage:
Two weeks before: The science teacher announced that models were due on the 15th. Vaibhav drew a quick volcano sketch and shoved it in his bag. His sister Uma started her own model that same weekend.
The night of the 14th: At nine o'clock Vaibhav remembered. He glued cardboard walls together, pasted on layers of wet newspaper and painted it brown while everything was still soaked. The glue shone. "It'll dry by morning," he said, and went to bed at midnight.
The 15th: In the morning the walls had slumped outward and the paper hung in soggy flaps. In the auto, one side fell off completely. Vaibhav carried the pieces into class in a plastic bag, and his ears burned when the teacher asked what had happened.

qa.q: What do Vaibhav's burning ears suggest?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and ashamed, carrying his model in pieces into class.

qa.q: What would you change first in Vaibhav's plan?
qa.a: Starting early, as Uma did, so there are a few days left for glue and paint to dry before the due date.

qa.q: How might Uma see Vaibhav's night-before rush?
qa.a: Uma started on the first weekend, so she might feel sorry for him but not very surprised.

grounding: Over two weeks, a boy leaves his model until the last night, glues it wet and finds it collapsed in the morning.

subtype: Approach: rushing to finish before the deadline [Pitfall]
passage: Jasleen, your project is due Friday and today is Monday? Good. Let me tell you about your Papa. When Uday was eleven, he had three weeks to make a model of the solar system. He played cricket for all three. On the last night he glued foam balls onto wires, painted them, and stuck everything onto a board at eleven o'clock. The glue was still white and wet when he went to bed. I said, "Leave it under the fan." He said, "It's fine." In the morning Saturn had slid down its wire and Jupiter was stuck to the Sun. He cried all the way to school, holding the broken board. After that, he started his projects the day he got them.

qa.q: How long did Uday have to make the model?
How did Uday feel on the way to school?
qa.a: He cried all the way, upset and ashamed of the broken board.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story would you change?
qa.a: Spending all three weeks on cricket; starting even a few days earlier would have left time for the glue to dry.

qa.q: How might the elder have felt watching Uday that morning?
qa.a: The elder had warned about the fan and probably felt sad for him, while hoping he would learn from it.

grounding: An elder recalls a boy who rushed his model on the last night and found the wet glue had let it fall apart by morning.
